title: Making a picture in my head
keyIdea: As you read or listen, build a picture in your head from the details in the words: what is there, where it is, and how many. Change the picture when a new sentence changes something. If the picture stops fitting the words, stop and reread. For a maths problem, keep the picture simple, like dots for posts and lines for gaps. Picturing what you read helps you understand it and remember it later.
familyTip: At bedtime, read a page aloud and pause. Ask: what does your picture look like? Where is everyone? Then read on and ask what changed. For a maths word problem, sketch it together with dots and lines, not a pretty drawing.

visual.caption: Does it help you make a good picture in your head? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Change it when the story changes
Add things the words never say
Reread when it does not fit
Draw every leaf for a maths problem

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build a harbour from the words, change it as the story changes, catch a picture that does not fit, solve with dots and gaps, rebuild a room.

kid: Good readers make pictures in their heads as they read. The words tell you what to put in your picture: what is there, where it is, and how many. If the words say the cat is on the roof of the boat, your cat goes on the roof, not on the jetty.
Stories change as you read. When a new sentence says the cat jumps onto the jetty, move the cat in your picture. If you keep your first picture, it will not match the story any more.
Sometimes your picture does not fit the words. Maybe the words said two balls and you pictured three. That is a sign to stop, read the sentence again, and fix your picture.

Pictures help with maths too, but keep them simple. For five posts in a row, draw five dots and the gaps between them. Then you can see there are only four gaps. A picture also helps you remember: you can look back at it in your head later.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This is a learning-to-learn skill. Children practise making mental images while reading. They use the images to check that they understand, to solve word problems and to remember. Key words: picture, detail, position, change, check, reread, simple diagram.

The evidence is good for children of this age. Pressley (1976) taught 8-year-olds to make a picture in their heads for each part of a story. They then answered more questions about it than children who just read it. Gambrell and Bales (1986) asked weak readers aged 9 to 11 to picture what they read. They noticed more of the parts of a text that did not make sense. The EEF guide on metacognition (2021) supports teaching such skills openly, with practice.

For maths, the kind of picture matters. Hegarty and Kozhevnikov (1999) found that pupils who pictured where things were and how many solved more problems. Pupils who pictured how things looked did not do better. So common mistakes are reading on without a picture, keeping the first picture when the story changes, and ignoring a picture that does not fit. Others are drawing pretty details, and counting posts when you need the gaps. Be careful not to add details the words do not give.

In the lab your child reads about a harbour and drags a boat, a cat, a gull and a crab to where the words say. Then three new sentences change the scene. They tap the part of a robot's picture that does not fit the words, in three pictures. They pick a dots-and-gaps picture to solve a posts problem (8 m) and a line problem (6 behind Sam). Last, they hide the words and rebuild a bedroom from memory.

practice.prompt: You read: "The dog hid under the table." Where is the dog in your picture?
practice.hint: Look at the word that tells you where: under.
practice.explain: Under means below. The word 'under' tells you exactly where to put the dog in your picture.

practice.prompt: {a} posts stand in a row, with 1 metre between each post and the next. How far is it from the first post to the last?
practice.hint: Draw the posts as dots. Count the gaps between the dots, not the dots.
practice.explain: {a} posts make {=a-1} gaps, and each gap is 1 metre, so it is {=a-1} metres from the first post to the last.

practice.prompt: The story says the cat is asleep on the bed. Then: "The cat jumps down and runs to the door." What do you do?
choices: Move the cat to the door in my picture
Keep the cat on the bed
practice.hint: A new sentence can change your picture.
practice.explain: Move the cat to the door. When the story changes, change your picture so it still matches.

practice.prompt: {a} children stand in a line. Ben is 2nd from the front. How many children are behind Ben?
practice.hint: Picture the line as dots. Count Ben and the child in front of him, then the rest.
practice.explain: Ben and the 1 child in front make 2. That leaves {=a-2} children behind Ben.

practice.prompt: Your picture shows a red boat, but you read that the boat is blue. What should you do?
practice.hint: When the picture and the words do not match, which one do you trust?
practice.explain: Reread and fix your picture. A picture that does not fit the words is a sign to check.

pool.prompt: Why make a picture in your head while you read?
choices: It helps me understand and remember
So I can add my own things
pool.hint: Think about what you can do with the picture after reading.
pool.explain: A picture helps you understand what you read and remember it later. It should come from the words, not extra things.

pool.prompt: Which picture helps most with a problem about 6 trees in a row?
choices: Six dots with gaps between them
A drawing of the park and the sky
pool.hint: Keep only what matters for the question: how many and where.
pool.explain: Six dots with gaps. Leaves and sky look nice but do not help you count.

pool.prompt: {a} lamp posts stand in a row, 5 metres apart. How far is it from the first post to the last?
pool.hint: Draw dots for the posts. Count the gaps, then each gap is 5 metres.
pool.explain: {a} posts make {=a-1} gaps, and {=a-1} gaps of 5 metres make {=5*(a-1)} metres.

pool.prompt: You read: "A bird sat between two cats." Which detail matters most for your picture?
pool.hint: Look for the word that tells you where.
pool.explain: Where the bird is: between the two cats. Position words build the picture.

pool.prompt: Your picture does not fit the sentence you just read. What is the best move?
pool.hint: A mismatch is a signal, not something to skip.
pool.explain: Stop and reread. Good readers notice when the picture and the words do not fit, then fix it.

pool.prompt: {a} children stand in a line. Mia is 3rd from the front. How many children are behind Mia?
pool.hint: Picture dots. Mia is the 3rd dot. Count the dots after her.
pool.explain: 2 children are in front of Mia, then Mia, so {=a-3} children stand behind her.

pool.prompt: You must remember where 4 things are in a room, and the words will be hidden. What helps most?
choices: Make a picture of the room in my head
Look at only the first word
pool.hint: Think about which one you can look back at later.
pool.explain: A picture of the room. You can look at it again in your head when the words are gone.

pool.prompt: The words say: "Two gulls sat on the roof." Your picture has three gulls. What is wrong?
pool.hint: Count the gulls in the words, then in your picture.
pool.explain: The number is wrong: the words say two gulls. Numbers are details to check in your picture.
